etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English bee, from Old English bēo, from Proto-West Germanic *bijā, from Proto-Germanic *bijō, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰey-.

definitions.definition: A flying insect, of the clade Anthophila within the hymenopteran superfamily Apoidea, known for its organised societies (though only a minority have them), for collecting pollen and (in some species) producing wax and honey.

quote.citation: 1499, John Skelton, The Bowge of Courte:
quote.text: His face was belymmed as byes had him stounge […].

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book III, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: An angry Wasp th'one in a viall had, / Th'other in hers an hony-laden Bee.

quote.citation: 1603, Michel de Montaigne, chapter 12, in John Florio, transl., The Essayes […], book II, London:  […]  Val[entine] Simmes for Edward Blount […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Can there be a more formall, and better ordered policie, divided into so severall charges and offices, more constantly entertained, and better maintained, than that of Bees?

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i], page 17:
quote.text: Ariell: / Where the Bee ſucks, there ſuck I, / In a Cowslips bell, I lie, / There I cowch when Owles doe crie, / On the Batts backe I doe flie / after Sommer merrily. / Merrily, merrily, ſhall I liue now / Vnder the bloſſom that hangs on the Bow.

quote.citation: 1657, Samuel Purchas, “The Excellency of Bees”, in A Theatre of Politicall Flying-Insects. […], London:  […]  R. I. for Thomas Parkhurst, […], →OCLC, page 1:
quote.text: Bees are the moſt excellent of all Inſects vvhatſoever, and expreſſe both vvorth and vvonder in all their vvaies:  […]
Bees pollinate many of the world’s crops—a service estimated to be worth $15 billion a year in America alone.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Possibly from dialectal bene, been, bean (“help given by neighbours”), from Middle English been, bene (“neighbourly help, prayer, petition, request, extra service given by a tenant to his lord”), from Old English bēn (“prayer, request, petition, favour, compulsory service”), from Proto-Germanic *bōniz (“prayer, request, supplication”). Thus a variant of obsolete ben (“prayer; petition”) and doublet of boon. Cognate with Danish bøn (“prayer”), Dutch ban (“curse”), German Bann (“ban”). More at ban.

definitions.definition: A contest, especially for spelling; see spelling bee.
A community gathering to share labour, e.g. a sewing bee or a quilting bee.

quote.citation: 1856, Samuel Griswold Goodrich, Recollections of a Lifetime:
quote.text: The cellar  […]  was dug by a bee in a single day.

quote.citation: 1973, Alan Skeoch, Tony H. Smith, Canadians and their society, page 139:
quote.text: There was but little variation in types of buildings in the pioneer period: house, church, store, barn and mill were usually much alike except in size, and a raising bee was the ordinary means of their erection.

quote.citation: 2011 September 21, Tim Blanning, “The reinvention of the night”, in Times Literary Supplement:
quote.text: Particularly resistant, for example, in many parts of northern Europe was the “spinning bee”, a nocturnal gathering of women to exchange gossip, stories, refreshment and – crucially – light and heat, as they spun wool or flax, knitted or sewed.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English beeȝ, bie, bei, begh, beiȝe, bege, beah, bye, from Old English bēah, bēag, from Proto-Germanic *baugaz. Doublet of beag, a learned borrowing; and of bagel.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A ring or torque; a bracelet.

quote.citation: 1485, Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte Darthur, Caxton, Book 7, Chapter xxxv:
quote.text: And kyng Arthur gaf her a ryche bee of gold and soo she departed

quote.citation: 1658, Sir Thomas Browne, Urne-Burial, Penguin, published 2005, page 16:
quote.text: ...restoring unto the world much gold richly adorning his Sword, two hundred Rubies, many hundred Imperial Coynes, three hundred golden Bees, the bones and horseshoe of his horse enterred with him...
held that a ‘Nicholaitan is an heretike, like Nicholas, who held that wiues should bee common to all alike.’

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 19, page 8:
quote.text: His Lady sad to see his sore constraint, / Cride out, Now now Sir knight, shew what ye bee / Add faith vnto your force, and be not faint: / Strangle her, els she sure will strangle thee.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English [Term?], from Old English be, from Latin be (the name of the letter B).

definitions.definition: The name of the Latin-script letter B/b.

quote.citation: 2004, Will Rogers, The Stonking Steps, page 170:
quote.text: "The ee-vee-ee-ar-en-oh-ee-ell-blank-bee-ell-oh-ess-ess-oh-em-blank-en-ee-cee-tee-ay-ar is especially dee-ee-ell-eye-cee-eye-oh-you-ess." Our friends thanked the spelling bee for his help and then he buzzed off.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Probably from Old English bēah (“ring”). Compare bow.

definitions.definition: (nautical, usually in the plural) Any of the pieces of hard wood bolted to the sides of the bowsprit, to reeve the fore-topmast stays through.
